question_text: A 6-year-old boy presents to your office with loss of his peripheral vision. His mother discovered this because he was almost struck by a vehicle that "he couldn't see at all". In addition, he has been complaining of a headache for the last several weeks and had an episode of vomiting 2 days ago. He has a family history of migraines in his mother and grandmother. He is currently in the 80th percentile for height and weight. On physical exam his temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 19/min, and pulse oximetry is 99% on room air. He is uncooperative for the rest of the physical exam. During workup, a lesion is found in this patient. Which of the following would most likely be seen during histopathologic analysis?

                    ### Question
                    A 6-year-old boy presents to your office with loss of his peripheral vision. His mother discovered this because he was almost struck by a vehicle that "he couldn't see at all". In addition, he has been complaining of a headache for the last several weeks and had an episode of vomiting 2 days ago. He has a family history of migraines in his mother and grandmother. On physical exam his temperature is 99°F (37.2°C), blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 19/min, and pulse oximetry is 99% on room air. He is uncooperative for the rest of the physical exam. During workup, a lesion is found in this patient. Which of the following would most likely be seen during histopathologic analysis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rosettes and small blue cells
opb. Eosinophilic, corkscrew fibers
opc. Perivascular rosettes with rod-shaped blepharoplasts
opd. Cholesterol crystals and calcification
ope. Round nuclei with clear cytoplasm

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of a 6-year-old boy with loss of peripheral vision, headaches, and vomiting suggests increased intracranial pressure, likely due to a mass effect. The location of the lesion near the optic chiasm points towards a suprasellar mass, such as a craniopharyngioma. Craniopharyngiomas are known to cause compression of the optic chiasm, leading to bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of peripheral vision). Histopathologically, craniopharyngiomas are characterized by the presence of cholesterol crystals and calcification. The retrieved evidence path supports the consideration of pituitary or suprasellar masses affecting the optic chiasm, aligning with the consensus that craniopharyngiomas are associated with these histological findings. Therefore, the most likely histopathologic finding in this case is 'Cholesterol crystals and calcification,' which corresponds to option 'opd.'
